Effrontery
ĕf-frŭn´tẽr-y
n. (shamelessness; impudence in doing or saying what should cause a blush)
French effronterie, from Latin ex-, out, and frons, the forehead — the brow that cannot be made to redden. Scripture's own figure is identical: a forehead of brass, a face that will not blush.

Biblical Definition

Effrontery is the loss of the capacity for shame. Jeremiah names it as a stage in a nation's decline: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush” (Jer 6:15, repeated at Jer 8:12). Ezekiel is sent to “impudent children and stiffhearted” (Eze 2:4). Proverbs shows it in the strange woman, who “caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him” (Pro 7:13). Paul describes men “whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Php 3:19). And Isaiah records Sodom's last stage: “they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not” (Isa 3:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines effrontery as impudence; audaciousness; shamelessness; assurance; a modest man may show a becoming boldness, but an impudent man only can be guilty of effrontery.

EFFRONTERY, n. Impudence; audaciousness; shamelessness; boldness; sauciness.

It is impudence and effrontery that supply the place of merit.

Effrontery is a sure mark of ill-breeding, and often of guilt.

Key Scripture

Jer 6:15 — "Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the LORD."

Eze 2:4 — "For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD."

Pro 7:13 — "So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him,"

Php 3:19 — "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)"

Isa 3:9 — "The shew of their countenance doth witness against them; and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not. Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves."

Modern Corruption

Shamelessness is mistaken for courage, and the inability to blush is a symptom rather than a strength.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 6:15 describes a specific and late stage of moral decline and its wording is careful: they were not ashamed, neither could they blush. Not would not — could not. The faculty had gone. Shame in Scripture is not the same as guilt: guilt is the objective state and shame is the God-given signal that registers it, and a conscience seared over time stops producing the signal while the state remains. That is why the loss is worse than the sin that caused it. A man who feels nothing has lost the alarm, not the fire.

The modern confusion runs the other way and it is worth naming, because shame has become a word almost entirely negative in usage. There is a false shame that Scripture works to destroy — the shame the forgiven feel over sins that are covered, the shame imposed by other people's judgments, the shame of the gospel that Paul refuses (I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ). Destroying that is a mercy. But a Christianity that treats every experience of shame as an injury to be healed has no vocabulary left for Jeremiah's diagnosis, and will read the inability to blush as freedom.

Philippians 3:19 gives the terminal form: whose glory is in their shame. Not indifference to shame but pride in it — the thing that once would have been hidden is now the boast, and the sequence in Isaiah 3:9 is the same, since the last step before judgment is that they declare their sin and hide it not. The remedy in every case is the same one Ezekiel was sent with, which is the word of God delivered to hard foreheads by a prophet God warned in advance that they would not listen — and told to speak anyway.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kalam (H3637), to be ashamed, confounded; bosh (H954), to blush, be ashamed; az panim (H5810, H6440), hard of face, impudent; Greek aischune (G152), shame.

Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, to blush; Jeremiah 6:15, 8:12, Ezra 9:6.

Hebrew chazqe metsach (H2389, H4696) — hard of forehead, impudent; Ezekiel 2:4, 3:7–9.

Greek aischune (G152) — shame; Philippians 3:19, Hebrews 12:2, Jude 1:13.

Usage

"“Neither could they blush” — could not, and that is the diagnosis."

"“Whose glory is in their shame” — the terminal form."

"“They declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not”."
